chapter.title: NCERT Class 10 English (First Flight - Complete Foundational Analysis)

grammar.explanation: Relative clauses give additional information about a noun using relative pronouns like who, which, that, whose, where.
examples: Lencho was a farmer who had unwavering faith in God. (Defining)
The postmaster, who was a fat and amiable fellow, decided to answer the letter. (Non-defining)

grammar.explanation: Nouns can be formed from verbs by adding suffixes such as -tion, -ment, -ance, -ence, -ion.
'Used to' expresses past states or repeated actions, whereas 'would' expresses repeated past actions in narrative context.
examples: The baker used to be our friend, companion, and guide. (Past state/habit)
Mijbil would jump and roll in the bathtub for hours. (Repeated past action)

grammar.explanation: Transforming spoken dialogue into reported clauses by shifting tenses (present to past), updating pronouns, and selecting appropriate reporting verbs.
examples: Direct: Lomov said, 'I've come to ask the hand of your daughter.'
Indirect: Lomov stated that he had come to ask for the hand of his daughter in marriage.

grammar.explanation: Nouns can act as modifiers preceding other nouns to specify function, material, or origin.
grammar.source_context: NCERT Class 10 English - Chapter 2, 5, 6 (jeff102.pdf, jeff105.pdf, jeff106.pdf)

spelling.rule_or_note: Poets intentionally alter standard spellings to preserve rhythm, meter, and humorous rhyme.
spelling.source_context: Carolyn Wells - How to Tell Wild Animals (jeff103.pdf)

spelling.standard_spelling: Amphitheatre (British) vs Amphitheater (American); Colour (British) vs Color (American)
spelling.rule_or_note: NCERT texts adhere strictly to standard UK/Commonwealth English spellings.

word_usage.nuance: 'Downpour' indicates a heavy, intense rainstorm; 'shower' denotes a light, gentle rain.
word_usage.example: The earth needed a downpour or at least a shower.

word_usage.nuance: 'Emancipation' specifically refers to legal/political liberation from systemic bondage, whereas 'freedom' is broader.
word_usage.example: We pledge to liberate all our people from the continuing bondage of poverty and emancipation.

word_usage.nuance: Refers to off-peak hours during business operations when activity is minimal.
word_usage.example: The afternoon 1 to 4 PM was the bus conductor's slack time.

sentence_structure.example: These aren't raindrops falling from the sky, they are new coins.

sentence_structure.pattern: Not only [Clause A], but also [Clause B]
sentence_structure.example: Not only was my own freedom curtailed, but the freedom of everyone who looked like I did was also restricted.

sentence_structure.pattern: Main narrative stanza followed by (Parenthetical internal monologue)
sentence_structure.example: (There is a languid, emerald sea, where the sole inhabitant is me— a mermaid, drifting blissfully.)

idioms_expressions.expression: Paper has more patience than people

literary_devices.definition: A sharp contrast between expected outcome and actual reality.
literary_devices.example: Lencho calls the post office workers 'a bunch of crooks' after they anonymously donated their own money to help him.

literary_devices.definition: A metaphor that unfolds across an entire poem or passage.
literary_devices.example: Carl Sandburg's comparison of fog to a cat moving on 'little cat feet' and sitting on 'quiet haunches'.

literary_devices.definition: Freedom taken by a poet to depart from standard grammar or spelling to achieve meter or rhyme.
literary_devices.example: Carolyn Wells spelling 'leapt' as 'lept' and 'dying' as 'dyin''.
literary_devices.source_context: Chapter 3 - How to Tell Wild Animals (jeff103.pdf)

literary_devices.definition: Literary work where natural elements symbolize women's social struggle for liberation.
literary_devices.example: Adrienne Rich's 'The Trees' depicting indoor trees breaking glass to reclaim the forest.

literary_devices.definition: Pairing contradictory terms or contrasting scenes side-by-side.
literary_devices.example: Leslie Norris pairing 'quiet rage' to describe the confined tiger in 'A Tiger in the Zoo'.
literary_devices.source_context: Chapter 2 - A Tiger in the Zoo (jeff102.pdf)
